It drops in asyour HTTP client.

Connected, the request goes straight to your origin over normal HTTPS. Disconnected, the same call is sealed, relayed device to device, and terminated at an endpoint you run. Call sites do not change.

01 · The swap

Replace the transport, not the app.

Hop implements the HTTP interface your app already uses. There is no new client library to learn and no data model to adopt.

The fast path stays boring, which is the point. When there is connectivity, nothing is sealed, nothing is queued, nothing is relayed, and no latency is added. That covers the overwhelming majority of traffic. You only pay for the machinery in the moments you would otherwise have failed.

Android · OkHttp interceptor 
// existing Retrofit / OkHttp setup, one line added
val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addInterceptor(HopInterceptor(node, endpoint = "hops://api.example.com"))
    .build()

// every existing call site is unchanged
api.submitTimeEntry(entry)
iOS · URLProtocol 
// register once at launch
URLProtocol.registerClass(HopURLProtocol.self)
HopURLProtocol.configure(node: node, endpoint: "hops://api.example.com")

// existing URLSession calls are unchanged
let (data, response) = try await URLSession.shared.data(for: request)
React Native · fetch adapter 
// wrap the global once
globalThis.fetch = hopFetch(globalThis.fetch, {
  node,
  endpoint: "hops://api.example.com",
  deferrable: ["POST /time-entries", "POST /forms", "PATCH /visits/*"],
})

The only genuinely new thing in those snippets is the last one: a list of which routes are allowed to arrive late. That list is the whole integration decision, and it is discussed under routing policy.

02 · What is underneath

One narrow waist, many bearers.

Hop is a delay-tolerant network in the Bundle Protocol lineage. Everything rides one sealed store-and-forward datagram, so the app above and the radio below can change independently.

Your appUnchanged. HTTP semantics through the client you already use
hops://HTTP over the mesh. Resolves to your endpoint's key, not an IP. The endpoint is bound to one origin and is never an open proxy
hdp://The waist. Sealed, signed, addressed store-and-forward datagrams. Relays carry ciphertext they cannot read
BearerBLE primary, plus direct channel, LAN and internet relay. Passive discovery, no pairing, so no user gesture per peer
DriverA thin per-platform shim runs the radios. The core is bearer-agnostic and sees only opaque link ids
Two properties that matter for your integration

Address is identity. A node is an Ed25519 keypair and its public key is its address, so you can verify a signature and seal to a peer with nothing but the address.

The fabric is shared. Any Hop app relays for any other, so peer density is not limited to your own install base.

Stated non-goals, read them before designing

Not low latency: lifetime is hours to days, not milliseconds. Not exactly-once: delivery is at-least-once with idempotency. Both of those shape everything below.

03 · Routing policy

Mark what is allowed to arrive late.

A transparent wrapper that silently makes fetch hang for an hour would break every timeout, spinner and retry in your app. So the client does not guess. You declare intent per route.

ClassBehaviour offlineTypical routes
deferrableAccepted locally, returns immediately with an idempotency key, delivered when a path existsSubmitting a record, a form, a photo, a status change, an append
live-onlyFails fast, exactly as it does todayFresh lists, search, pricing, availability, anything a stale answer would corrupt
arbitratedFails fast even though it is a write, because the server must decideClaiming a contended resource, the last slot, a lock, a booking race
The mistake to avoid

Do not mark a contended write deferrable. Two devices optimistically claiming one slot produces a double booking that is your bug and ours. If a write needs arbitration, it needs the server, and the honest answer offline is a clear failure.

04 · The layer

CQRS and optimistic responses belong here, not in your app.

This is what makes the swap honest rather than a lie. Commands return immediately. Queries answer from a local projection. Reconciliation applies the authoritative response whenever it lands. The lifecycle is observable, so your UI can be truthful instead of showing a spinner and hoping.

01StoredAccepted locally with an idempotency key. A synthetic accepted response returns and your code proceeds
02In flightSealed and handed to the mesh. Held under custody, not dropped
03Server receivedYour endpoint ran it against the real API and acknowledged
04SettledAccepted, or rejected with a reason. Divergence from the local projection raises an event
Subscribing to the lifecycle 
hop.observe(entry.idempotencyKey) { state in
  switch state {
  case .stored:         ui.show("Saved on this device")
  case .inFlight:       ui.show("On its way")
  case .serverReceived: ui.show("We have it")
  case .settled(let r): ui.reconcile(r)   // may differ from the projection
  }
}
Where optimistic is correct

Facts the user owns: they performed the action, and the server's job is to record it, not to authorise it. A clock event, a form, a photo, an incident note. Not a claim on something somebody else might also claim.

05 · Your server side

Five changes, all small, none optional.

What has to be true on your API
RequirementWhyShape
Idempotency key on deferrable writesDelivery is at-least-once, so the same record can arrive twice by independent pathsA header plus a uniqueness constraint. The pattern Stripe normalised
Tolerate out-of-order arrivalIndependent paths mean a finish can land before its startOrder by claimed event time, not receipt time. Accept and reorder rather than reject
Separate claimed time from receipt timeThe device asserts when it happened. Your server knows when it heard. Both are facts and they are different factsTwo columns, and a documented conflict rule
Authenticate the device keyA bearer token may expire before a bundle from this morning landsBind the Ed25519 address to the account at enrolment and verify the signature
Run an endpoint in front of the APIIt terminates hops:// against your own origin, on your infrastructure, bound to one domainOne service, no third party in the path
Sequencing note

Idempotency and the claimed/receipt split are worth doing whether or not you ever ship Hop. They are the two changes that make any offline-capable client safe, and most APIs that have been burned by retries already have the first one.

06 · Never the sole path

Things that must not ride this.

  • Anything unsafe without current server state, including urgent expiry and matching.
  • Identity proofing, sanctions, right-to-work or credential revocation decisions needing a fresh authoritative query.
  • Payment authorisation, stored value, settlement or filing.
  • Automatic check-in or check-out of any kind.
  • Continuous location traces, or live location after acceptance.
  • Account restriction, suspension, termination or final adverse action.
  • Any deadline defined by a server, a regulator or a third party's receipt.
Privacy is a requirement, not yet a finished control

End-to-end encryption hides payload from relays. It does not by itself hide radio presence, timing, packet size, encounter patterns or a stable discovery identifier. Minimise payloads, prefer assertions over source documents, set short event-specific lifetimes rather than inheriting a default, and scope keys so a lost relay cannot become a reader.

07 · Guardrails

The transport carries bytes. It decides nothing.

These are design constraints, not preferences. Crossing one changes what the product legally is, and in some jurisdictions it walks into somebody else's patent claims.

  • No location-triggered timer. Detection, proximity, encounter, discovery, NFC or geofence entry never starts or operates a clock automatically.
  • No generated geofence. Sites and radii are owned and configured by the operator, persistently, never derived per task.
  • No approval-caused activation. A supervisor may dispute a record later. Approval never starts the clock.
  • No live location after acceptance.
  • No encounter-triggered matching. Peers may move an already-authorised snapshot. They may not discover or rank people for work.
  • No route-derived signal. Hop count, relay identity, device density, delivery speed and custody behaviour must never influence matching, rating, discipline or pay.

08 · Prove it before you plan it

The bench test is cheap and it is the real gate.

Background BLE relay on iOS is the single biggest technical risk in this whole design. Do not take it on faith and do not take it from us. Measure it.

StepSetupPass condition
One hop, backgroundedTwo devices, one with connectivity fully off, both apps backgrounded, realistic spacingThe record lands, and you can see which path it took
Per OS and device classRepeat across your actual supported matrix, including old hardwareAdvertise, discover, relay and acknowledge before expiry on the large majority of devices
BatteryA full shift with the radios activeA drain your users will not notice and your support team will not hear about
Custody pressurePeak event volume against a constrained storePriority events are not evicted before they expire
Incremental valueCompare Hop plus local queue against a local queue aloneA materially larger share of records land during the shift, with no duplicate state transitions
If the bench fails

Then peer relay is not available to you on this hardware, and the honest fallback is a durable local queue plus an always-on node at the site. That is a smaller product, and it is still better than what most apps ship today.

Code shapes on this pageillustrativeThey show the integration seam and the call-site impact. They are not copied from a shipped SDK surface

Hop is a delay-tolerant mesh: end-to-end encrypted datagrams that hop device to device, over Bluetooth, wifi and the internet, until they reach the person or service you meant. The device does the work, so the SDK is free. The hosted backbone is what costs money to run, and that is what you pay for, only when you use it.

Photography on this page is AI generated and illustrative. Code samples are illustrative of the integration seam rather than copied from a shipped SDK surface. Diagrams are drawn, not generated. Protocol statements are attributed to Hop's own design documents and public protocol pages, with their stated non-goals intact.
